title: The Fear of Success
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay pivots from the familiar fear of failure to a less-discussed phenomenon: the fear of success. It argues that once performers learn to use fear of failure productively, they can hit a second, often unconscious barrier as they approach their highest level of achievement -- a fear that continued success brings unsustainable pressure, scrutiny, and expectation. The piece walks through the psychological mechanics of this fear, including worries about peer jealousy and being exposed as limited, and identifies self-sabotage (procrastination, avoiding tough competition, declining opportunities) as the behavioral escape valve. It closes by arguing this fear is ultimately more destructive to high performers than fear of failure ever was.
points: A modest fear of failure can be productive, driving preparation and skill development -- but fear of success operates differently and often unconsciously.
Fear of success tends to emerge right as performers approach the pinnacle of achievement, when expectations and scrutiny are about to rise.
Performers gripped by this fear worry they can't sustain continued success and that others will discover their real limits.
Some performers also fear that continued success will create jealousy and damage relationships with peers.
Left unaddressed, the fear of success drives self-sabotage: procrastination, declining opportunities, and avoiding tougher competition.
quotes: Ironically, most performers owe their personal growth and success to a modest fear of failure.
Once a leader or performer has learned to tame the fear of failure, using it as a motivating force instead of as a performance inhibitor, they often face a newfound fear -- The Fear of Success.
They astutely recognize that continued success will increase the responsibility and work required to live up to the new bar set by high achievement.
They even have a concern that continued success will create peer jealousy and weaken their connection to friends and peers who lack the talent or opportunity to reach the same heights.
The fear of failure is nowhere near as destructive as the fear of success.
Instead, it is about admitting to themselves that more success comes with a package of pressure they do not want or are not ready to conquer.
